questions.q: Before volcanoes, floods and earthquakes, man and all his developments are helpless. What lesson does the article draw from this?
options: Nature is man’s enemy
Not quite. The article says: Man is not the master of this world and should live in it with modesty and humility.
Man is not the master of this world and should live in it with modesty and humility
Yes. Such experiences are there to be learned from.
Man should move to safer planets
Not quite. The article says: Man is not the master of this world and should live in it with modesty and humility.
Science has failed mankind
Not quite. The article says: Man is not the master of this world and should live in it with modesty and humility.
questions.rationale: “These natural experiences teach that man is not the master of this world. In this world man must lead a life of modesty and humility.”

questions.q: The Maulana saw many talented, highly educated people fail in practical life. What does he say held them back?
options: Jealous colleagues
Not quite. The article says: An exaggerated estimate of themselves, which made them look down on the tasks they were given.
An exaggerated estimate of themselves, which made them look down on the tasks they were given
Right. He calls each one “a case of overestimation.”
A lack of money at the start
Not quite. The article says: An exaggerated estimate of themselves, which made them look down on the tasks they were given.
Poor health in youth
Not quite. The article says: An exaggerated estimate of themselves, which made them look down on the tasks they were given.
questions.rationale: “The exaggerated assessment of their ability and talent did not allow them to do anything worthwhile. They could not adapt to the tasks they were assigned, because they considered them of lesser status.”

questions.q: A student lost two years to a spinal injury and thought his life was over. Which insight gave him the courage to return and come first?
options: Others have suffered more
Not quite. The article says: Even if a man’s past and present are destroyed, his future is still intact.
Even if a man’s past and present are destroyed, his future is still intact
Well read. And: don’t use an excuse, even a good one.
Fortune favours the brave
Not quite. The article says: Even if a man’s past and present are destroyed, his future is still intact.
Time heals every wound
Not quite. The article says: Even if a man’s past and present are destroyed, his future is still intact.
questions.rationale: “Don’t use an excuse, even if it is a good one; even if a man’s past and present are destroyed, his future is still intact.”

questions.q: A magazine cover described a fallen president as “A Man without a Country.” Why did the Maulana feel this was every man’s story?
options: Everyone travels abroad at some time
Not quite. The article says: Death separates each person from whatever he has become lord of, and he goes on to the Hereafter with nothing.
Death separates each person from whatever he has become lord of, and he goes on to the Hereafter with nothing
Well reasoned. Every “country” is held only for a time.
Rulers are always forgotten
Not quite. The article says: Death separates each person from whatever he has become lord of, and he goes on to the Hereafter with nothing.
Borders change in every age
Not quite. The article says: Death separates each person from whatever he has become lord of, and he goes on to the Hereafter with nothing.
questions.rationale: “In this world, every man has a country of which he has become the lord. However, death separates every man from his country.”

questions.q: King Roger II of Sicily invited the geographer Al-Idrisi to his court to make a map of the world. What does the article see in this as the way to esteem?
options: Having powerful friends
Not quite. The article says: Being useful to the world – having something of value that others need.
Demanding one’s rights loudly
Not quite. The article says: Being useful to the world – having something of value that others need.
Travelling widely
Not quite. The article says: Being useful to the world – having something of value that others need.
Being useful to the world – having something of value that others need
Yes. People seek out those who benefit them.
questions.rationale: “They had something that others did not have, so people flocked to their sides.”

questions.article: The Relationship Between Man and God
questions.q: “I am near. I respond to the call of one who calls” (2:186). How does the article describe the relationship between man and God?
options: Distant – reached only through others
Not quite. The article says: Reciprocal – man offers realization, piety and thankfulness, and God bestows guidance in return.
Reciprocal – man offers realization, piety and thankfulness, and God bestows guidance in return
Correct. “Let them, then, respond to Me.”
Uncertain – no one can know
Not quite. The article says: Reciprocal – man offers realization, piety and thankfulness, and God bestows guidance in return.
One-sided – man receives and owes nothing
Not quite. The article says: Reciprocal – man offers realization, piety and thankfulness, and God bestows guidance in return.
questions.rationale: “This shows that the relationship between man and God is reciprocal: man offers God what he has, then God bestows His favours in return.”

questions.q: To what does the article compare a dependable, tempered character in the building of a nation?
options: The roof that keeps out the rain
Not quite. The article says: Kiln-fired bricks, which can withstand storm and flood where unfired bricks collapse.
The paint on a finished house
Not quite. The article says: Kiln-fired bricks, which can withstand storm and flood where unfired bricks collapse.
The garden around a house
Not quite. The article says: Kiln-fired bricks, which can withstand storm and flood where unfired bricks collapse.
Kiln-fired bricks, which can withstand storm and flood where unfired bricks collapse
Right. Character is the building material.
questions.rationale: “A character so tempered that it can be depended upon through thick and thin like the kiln-fired brick is what in the long run builds a nation.”

questions.q: When newly built structures fail, more technical training is often proposed. Why does the article say this will not cure the problem?
options: Materials are the only problem
Not quite. The article says: The fault is moral, not technical – and a moral fault cannot be removed by technical improvement.
The fault is moral, not technical – and a moral fault cannot be removed by technical improvement
Exactly. It calls for the reform of individuals.
Training takes too long
Not quite. The article says: The fault is moral, not technical – and a moral fault cannot be removed by technical improvement.
There are already too many engineers
Not quite. The article says: The fault is moral, not technical – and a moral fault cannot be removed by technical improvement.
questions.rationale: “Corruption is a psychological evil, while lack of skill is a technical shortcoming. A psychological evil cannot be removed by technical improvement.”

questions.q: A passenger misses his train and a porter tells him to wait for the next. What is “the lesson that the platform teaches”?
options: A missed opportunity is not the end; there is always a “next train” for one who waits patiently and stays alert
Yes. A God-given second opportunity.
Always arrive two hours early
Not quite. The article says: A missed opportunity is not the end; there is always a “next train” for one who waits patiently and stays alert.
Travel by another means
Not quite. The article says: A missed opportunity is not the end; there is always a “next train” for one who waits patiently and stays alert.
Never trust a watch
Not quite. The article says: A missed opportunity is not the end; there is always a “next train” for one who waits patiently and stays alert.
questions.rationale: “When we miss a train, there is always the comforting knowledge that there is that next train coming along. That is the lesson that the platform teaches.”

questions.q: How does the article define real charity?
options: That which is given for God’s sake alone, not for fame, self-esteem or worldly reward
Well read. Giving as thanks for what one has been given.
That which is given in public
Not quite. The article says: That which is given for God’s sake alone, not for fame, self-esteem or worldly reward.
That which is given to relatives only
Not quite. The article says: That which is given for God’s sake alone, not for fame, self-esteem or worldly reward.
That which is given in the largest amount
Not quite. The article says: That which is given for God’s sake alone, not for fame, self-esteem or worldly reward.
questions.rationale: “Real charity is that which is given for God’s sake alone, not for fame, self-esteem or worldly reward.”
